Helm 1814 says only that his wife was among 'squaws' and does not mention the rescue.
persons.fate: His village was later destroyed 'in a single day' (Andreas); ransomed Lt Helm from the Kankakee with pony, rifle and nose ring (Andreas, unsourced there).

camp_population.miami_not_in_camp: Wells's ~30 Miamis are not placed in the Potawatomi camp by any source; keep them separate (near the fort, with ponies) as reconstructed.
camp_population.recommendation: Total on the ground on 14 Aug: roughly 680-800 people (Helm's 679 on the 12th; the Gazette's ~800 at the distribution). Men outnumber women and children about 5:2 in Helm's count, which likely undercounts children. A respectful representative scene might draw about one figure per ten to fifteen people: 45-70 figures across the six camp grounds, about two-thirds adult men and one-third women and children, plus a few Miami near the fort. Declare the count, the ratio and every placement reconstructed (L-1812 liberty), citing Helm and Heald for the totals.

notes: SOURCE TIERS. Contemporary: Heald's report (23 Oct 1812) and Journal, Helm's narrative (1814), Griffith/McAfee, the Missouri Gazette (19 Sept 1812), all read as printed in Quaife's appendices. Late recollection: Darius Heald to Draper (1868), Matson's Shabbona (1876), Hubbard. Family tradition: Wau-Bun (Mrs Helm and Mrs Kinzie via Juliette Kinzie). Quaife App. II (lines 15290-15320) says its speeches and dialogue are invented, and Mrs Heald (App. V, lines 16479-16480) called it exaggerated. Every Wau-Bun speech here, including Black Partridge's medal speech, the Miami chief's speech and Caldwell's 'Sau-ga-nash' exchange, is family tradition and must not be shown as attested dialogue. DATE CONFLICTS for the scene: Wells arrived on the 12th (Helm), the 13th (Heald, preferred) or the 14th (Wau-Bun). The goods were distributed on the 13th (Wau-Bun) or the 14th (Heald, preferred). Ammunition was destroyed the night of the 13th (Helm, Andreas, Wau-Bun); Heald does not date it. On the 14th Wau-Bun has a second council in the afternoon and Black Partridge's medal return that evening (Helm: 'the night of the 14th'). The Missouri Gazette brings Main Poc's runner with a red belt on the 14th. EDITIONS. kinzie_waubun_1856 line numbers are from Gutenberg #12183 (the 1873 Philadelphia printing, with footnotes updated to 1870). Chapter numbers match 1856, and the 1856 page numbers were not checked. Andreas line numbers are from the archive.org OCR (historyofchicago01andr_djvu.txt, downloaded to src/dl_andreas/), and page numbers come from the OCR's page headers, some of which are lost. Where a quote says 'OCR normalised', spacing and obvious OCR letter errors were corrected. KINZIE'S NATIVE CONNECTIONS: his Native name was Shaw-nee-aw-kee, glossed 'silver-smith' (Kirkland lines 2120-2121, 5132-5134; Wau-Bun ch. XIX line 5806 uses it in 1812). His protectors in Aug 1812 were Topenebe's St Joseph band, Kee-po-tah, Black Partridge, Waubansee and Caldwell; his clerk was Chandonnai, his servant the interpreter Le Claire, and he had Francois the interpreter and the Ouilmette household. Wau-Bun (lines 5304-5312) has the officers saying the chiefs' restraint came 'by motives of private regard to one family, that of Mr. Kinzie'. NOT FOUND: Mucktypoke as a spelling (Andreas has 'Muck-otey-pokee'); any name or meaning for Waubansee, Kee-po-tah, Pee-so-tum or Wau-bee-nee-mah; any named Miami of Wells's escort ('Corn Plant' is unsupported); any surviving Billy Caldwell portrait; any 1812 description specific to Potawatomi women's dress at Chicago. Not opened, so not cited: Clifton's The Prairie People, Edmunds's The Potawatomis, and the Newberry Indigenous Chicago curriculum beyond the one existing Robinson profile. PRESENCE VALUE 'uncertain' (Robinson) and 'unknown' (Co-wa-bee-mai) are added beyond the three requested values, because the evidence will not support a call either way.
